content: 1. The development of the guidelines involved several key steps, including the formulation of key questions, conducting systematic reviews of evidence to address these questions, assessing the certainty (or quality) of the evidence for critical outcomes, and drafting recommendations. 2. The guideline document was prepared for review and approval by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and underwent peer review. It was also reviewed and approved by the World Health Organization’s (WHO) quality assurance body before publication and dissemination. 3. A wide range of contributors participated in the development of these guidelines, including individuals with diverse expertise, experiences, and perspectives. Each contributor had a clearly defined role and adhered to specific WHO policies and procedures to ensure transparency and effectiveness. 4. The WHO Steering Group, composed of members from relevant technical units at WHO headquarters and regional offices, provided technical guidance, project management, and administrative support throughout the process. 5. The GDG finalized the scope and key questions for the guidelines and developed the recommendations. Members of the GDG represented all WHO regions and brought expertise in managing chronic pain in children, including human rights law, bioethics, social policy, and lived experiences with chronic pain. 6. Systematic review teams, selected through an open competition, were contracted to provide evidence reviews. The External Review Group (ERG) attended recommendation-formulation meetings and provided input on the final content and presentation of the guidelines. 7. WHO required all internal and external contributors to undergo a thorough conflict-of-interest assessment before participating in the guideline development process. Only individuals without significant conflicts of interest were invited to join the GDG or ERG. 8. The GDG determined the scope of the guidelines, key questions for systematic reviews, and prioritized relevant outcomes. WHO commissioned systematic reviews of quantitative evidence on the benefits and harms of physical, psychological, and pharmacological interventions for chronic pain in children. 9. A second review examined qualitative evidence on the experiences and perceptions of patients, families, caregivers, and healthcare providers regarding these interventions. Barriers and facilitators to implementation were also analyzed. 10. The guidelines considered children of all ages, recognizing that their cognitive, social, and functional abilities evolve as they grow. Subgroup analyses were conducted wherever possible to account for these differences. 11. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system was used to assess the certainty of quantitative evidence for critical outcomes. GRADE-CERQual was used to evaluate confidence in qualitative evidence findings. 12. A systematic review of economic data, including costs and cost-effectiveness, was also conducted to inform the recommendations. 13. The GDG formulated recommendations during virtual meetings in September 2020, using a structured evidence-to-decision framework to ensure transparency and comprehensive discussions. 14. Recommendations were based on evidence of benefits, harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource considerations, and equity. They were categorized as either strong or conditional, depending on the level of certainty and consensus. 15. Strong recommendations indicated that most patients, caregivers, or providers would choose the intervention, while conditional recommendations required shared decision-making due to varying preferences. 16. The GDG reached consensus on recommendations through discussion. When consensus was not possible, anonymized voting was conducted, with an 80% approval threshold for adoption. 17. In addition to intervention recommendations, the guidelines included guiding principles based on human rights and ethics, as well as best practice statements for clinical care. These did not require systematic reviews but were grounded in good clinical practice and healthcare provider experience. 18. The guidelines also identified research gaps related to the management of chronic pain in children, derived from systematic reviews and GDG discussions. 19. Following the formulation of recommendations, the guidelines were drafted, reviewed, and approved by the GDG and ERG. They underwent further review by WHO’s Guidelines Review Committee before final publication and dissemination. 20. WHO commissioned three systematic reviews to provide evidence for the GDG’s decisions and recommendations. These reviews focused on the effectiveness of physical, psychological, and pharmacological interventions, as well as economic evaluations. 21. The systematic review of physical interventions included 25 studies, mostly randomized controlled trials (RCTs), examining therapies such as exercise, yoga, and hydrotherapy. Evidence suggested short-term benefits for pain intensity and functional disability but no long-term benefits. 22. The systematic review of psychological interventions included 63 RCTs, with evidence supporting small benefits for pain reduction, functional disability, and satisfaction post-treatment. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), relaxation training, and acceptance commitment therapy (ACT) were among the interventions studied. 23. The systematic review of pharmacological interventions included 34 studies examining drugs such as paracetamol, NSAIDs, and antidepressants. No eligible studies were found for opioids or ketamine. Evidence was limited and of low certainty. 24. Few studies reported adverse events for any intervention. For physical therapies, muscle soreness was noted but resolved within days. For psychological and pharmacological interventions, adverse events were infrequently reported. 25. The guidelines emphasized the importance of evidence-based, patient-centered approaches to managing chronic pain in children, with a focus on improving function and quality of life while minimizing harm.
